name: Cornaro low-calorie regimen

lead: The Cornaro regimen is the tiny-ration eating plan of Luigi (Alvise) Cornaro, a Venetian nobleman who, after feeling unwell in his forties, limited himself to a small, fixed daily amount of food and wine. His book on 'the sober life' made the case that moderation preserved health and vitality into old age.

People interested in anti-aging and longevity cite him as a historical forerunner of calorie restriction, with the appeal that staying lean and healthy supports a youthful appearance over the long term.

paras: Cornaro described his own routine: about 350 g of food a day (bread, egg yolk, meat, soup) and about 414 mL of wine, according to Wikipedia. Modern followers of calorie restriction discuss related ideas, but his regimen is a historical account rather than a protocol.

Wikipedia's calorie restriction article notes that sustained restriction can cause muscle loss, cold sensitivity and hormonal changes, and that moderate restriction may be harmful for lean people with low body fat. Cornaro's own age claims were partly exaggerated, and critics such as Nietzsche questioned whether the diet caused his longevity.

chain: Lower calorie intake and body weight
Lean, active body maintained into older age
angle.text: Followers see the regimen as a route to staying lean, energetic and youthful-looking for longer through sustained moderation. The case rests on Cornaro's own account of his health rather than controlled research.

lead: Luigi (Alvise) Cornaro (c. 1484 to 8 May 1566) was a Venetian nobleman, patron of the arts and author from Padua who built a fortune through land-reclamation projects and is best known for writing on how to live long [1]. In his forties he found himself exhausted and unwell, which he attributed to overindulgence, and on medical advice he adopted a strictly limited diet [1].

The regimen, as described, consisted of about 350 g of food a day, including bread, egg yolk, meat and soup, along with about 414 mL of wine [1]. He set out his reasoning in the Discorsi della vita sobria ('Discourses on the Sober Life'), which circulated widely and was praised by Joseph Addison in The Spectator for its cheerful, sensible tone [1].

Cornaro's claims of vigorous old age are central to his appeal for people interested in longevity and youthful appearance, though Wikipedia notes he overstated his age over time, and sources give his age at death as 98 or 102 [1]. Nietzsche criticized the work for confusing cause and effect, suggesting a slow metabolism could explain both the long life and the sparse diet [1]. The modern descendant of the idea is calorie restriction, which research has linked in animals to longer life, while evidence for preventing age-related disease in humans remains preliminary [2].
infobox: About 350 g food and 414 mL wine daily

paras: Cornaro adopted the regimen in his forties after poor health that he blamed on excess. He limited himself to roughly 350 g of food a day and about 414 mL of wine, and he wrote that it restored his health and kept him active into old age [1].

Cornaro was also a patron of the arts who sat for Tintoretto, supported the architect Giovanni Maria Falconetto, and knew the young Andrea Palladio [1]. His Discorsi della vita sobria spread his message, and Wikipedia lists its follow-up discourses as written in 1553, 1558 and 1562, although its dating of the publications is internally inconsistent [1]. Addison praised it in The Spectator, while Nietzsche argued it mistook cause for effect [1].

Calorie restriction, reducing intake by roughly 20 to 30 percent while meeting nutrient needs, has been linked to remedies for diseases of aging, though evidence that it prevents age-related disease in humans remains under preliminary research [2]. Reported risks include muscle wasting, cold sensitivity, menstrual irregularities and hormonal changes, and moderate restriction may be harmful for lean people with low body fat [2].
No studies found. Studies of the broader category of calorie restriction exist, including trials in humans, but none test Cornaro's specific regimen [2].

timeline.event: Luigi Cornaro born, most likely in Padua [1].
Cornaro says he is about 83 and remains healthy and active [1].
Cornaro dies on 8 May; age at death given as 98 or 102 [1].
